title: What you keep
hook: three Stoic habits that fit your life

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Chrysippus, who thought only the souls of the wise last until the world's burning. Your line was what it leaves open.

Open almost any kitchen drawer and you'll find the gadgets: a garlic press, an egg slicer, a cherry pitter used once. Then there's what actually gets reached for every night: one good knife, one pan, a wooden spoon. Nobody plans that short list. Use writes it. This year on the path has handed you a lot: morning previews, evening questions, two handles, two cities, the view from above, the ripe olive. Most of it can stay in the drawer.
screen: `A DRAWER FULL OF GADGETS.` → `ONE KNIFE, ONE PAN, ONE SPOON.` → `A YEAR OF PRACTICES.`

segments.voice: First, Seneca on books. In one of his earliest letters to Lucilius, he warns against reading too many authors, skipping from one to the next. Food thrown up as soon as it's swallowed doesn't nourish, he says, and a plant moved too often never grows. Better to stay with a few great minds and digest them, and each day choose one thought to carry. That's this week's spirit: not everything, but a few things, really digested. Second, Epictetus on training. The Stoic word is askēsis: practice, training, the way an athlete trains. Every habit, Epictetus says, is built up and strengthened by the matching actions: walking by walking, running by running. Want to be good at something? Do it. Don't want a habit? Stop feeding it. So the habits you keep are the ones you'll actually do, not the ones you admire. Third, how to choose your three. Ask three questions of each practice from the year. Did I actually use it? Did it change a real day, even once? Does it fit the life I have, with my work, my family, my body, my beliefs? Someone might keep the evening review, the two columns, and delaying an angry reply. Someone else, the morning preview, the view from above, and love for the mortal. There's no right three. Fourth, why three. Few enough to remember without a list, and enough to cover morning, evening and the hard moments between. Epictetus told his students not to talk about their principles, but to show them by how they live. Three is a number you can show.
screen: `DIGEST A FEW, DON'T SAMPLE MANY.` · `ASKĒSIS: HABITS BUILT BY DOING.` · `USED IT? CHANGED A DAY? FITS MY LIFE?` · `THREE YOU CAN SHOW, NOT TELL.` · then, large: `MY THREE.`

segments.voice: Let the year's practices pass slowly through your mind like utensils laid on a counter: the morning preview, the evening questions, the two columns, the other handle, the view from above, delay, both cities, begin now. Notice which ones your hand actually reached for on hard days, and pick up three, one at a time. Put the others back in the drawer; you're not throwing them away.
Askēsis, the Stoic word for practice and training, the habits worth keeping because you actually use them, not just admire them. Today's word.
Your line: my three. A few habits, used, outweigh a drawer full of admired ones. That's day six hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Some people finishing a period of Stoic study choose a small number of practices, often three, that they will keep using daily, and write them down.

askēsis.meaning: Greek for practice or training, the way an athlete trains

Epictetus.meaning: a Stoic teacher who said habits grow by matching actions

notes: Letters 2 paraphrased (food that comes up as soon as it's swallowed doesn't nourish; a plant often moved can't grow; stay with a few master thinkers; choose one thought each day). Confirm.
Discourses 2.18 (every habit confirmed by corresponding actions: walking by walking, running by running) and 3.12 (on training, askēsis). Confirm.
Enchiridion 46: don't call yourself a philosopher or talk about principles; act on them. Confirm.
